o: Comes from S2, S3 and S4

It is the main somatic nerve of the perineum.
It also supplies the external sphincters. (Last's p. 398, 411, 417)
Leaves the pelvis above piriformis

It leaves below piriformis through the greater sciatic foramen.
It then hooks round the sacrospinous ligament. (Last's p. 398, 411, 417)
Supplies the external anal sphincter through the pelvic splanchnic nerves

It supplies the sphincter through its inferior rectal branch.
The pelvic splanchnics are parasympathetic. (Last's p. 398, 411, 417)
Enters the perineum through the obturator canal

It enters through the lesser sciatic foramen into the pudendal canal.
The canal lies on obturator internus fascia. (Last's p. 398, 411, 417)
Has the deep ring medial to the inferior epigastric artery

The deep ring lies lateral to the inferior epigastric artery.
Direct hernias come through medial to it. (Last's)
Has the ilioinguinal nerve entering through the deep ring

The ilioinguinal enters by piercing internal oblique, not through the deep ring.
It then leaves through the superficial ring. (Last's)
Has the conjoint tendon as its anterior wall

The conjoint tendon reinforces the posterior wall medially.
The external oblique aponeurosis forms the anterior wall. (Last's)
Has the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve entering through the deep ring

The genital branch enters at the deep ring and runs in the spermatic cord.
It supplies cremaster. (Last's)
Receives the greater splanchnic nerves

Greater splanchnics (T5–9) pierce the crura to reach the coeliac ganglia.
Their fibres relay there. (Last's)
Receives vagal fibres

Vagal fibres pass through without relaying.
They relay in the walls of the organs.
Contains ganglia where sympathetic fibres relay

The coeliac ganglia are where preganglionic sympathetic fibres synapse.
Postganglionic fibres follow the arteries.
Carries pain from the foregut, referred to the epigastrium

Visceral afferents travel with the sympathetic fibres.
Foregut pain is felt in the epigastrium.
The superior hypogastric plexus lies in front of S3

It lies in front of L5 and the sacral promontory.
So "presacral nerve" is a misnomer: it is prelumbar. (Last's p. 365)
The inferior hypogastric plexus lies lateral to the rectum

It lies on the side wall of the pelvis lateral to the rectum.
It measures about 5 cm by 2 cm (Last's p. 399).
Parasympathetic fibres relay in the inferior hypogastric plexus

None of the parasympathetic fibres synapse in it.
They relay in ganglia in the organ walls (Last's p. 399).
Only about half of the sympathetic fibres synapse in the pelvic plexus

About half relay in the plexus; the rest have already relayed.
They relay in the lumbar or sacral sympathetic ganglia first (Last's p. 399).

questions.s: Concerning the nerve supply of the peritoneum:
o: The parietal peritoneum has a segmental supply from spinal nerves

Parietal serosa develops from somatopleure and is supplied segmentally by spinal nerves.
So it is sensitive to pain and well localised. (Last's)
The central diaphragmatic peritoneum is supplied by intercostal nerves

The central part is supplied by the phrenic nerve.
The peripheral part is supplied by intercostal nerves. (Last's)
In the pelvis the femoral nerve is the chief supply of the parietal peritoneum

In the pelvis the obturator nerve is the chief supply.
So pelvic peritonitis can cause pain on the medial thigh. (Last's)
The visceral peritoneum is supplied segmentally by spinal nerves

The visceral layer develops from splanchnopleure and is supplied by autonomic nerves, if at all.
It has no somatic sensory supply. (Last's)
The iliohypogastric nerve supplies the skin above the pubis

It supplies the suprapubic skin and part of the gluteal region.
It comes from L1. (Last's)
The subcostal nerve is T11

The subcostal nerve is T12.
It runs below the twelfth rib. (Last's)
The ilioinguinal nerve enters the inguinal canal through the deep ring

It pierces internal oblique and enters the canal from the side.
It leaves through the superficial ring. (Last's)
The genitofemoral nerve pierces quadratus lumborum

It pierces the front of psoas.
The subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal cross quadratus lumborum. (Last's)
Inserts into the greater trochanter

It inserts into the lesser trochanter.
It passes down along the pelvic brim and under the inguinal ligament into the thigh. (Last's)
Contains the lumbar plexus within its substance

The lumbar plexus forms within the muscle.
Its branches emerge from the lateral and medial borders and the front. (Last's)
Has the obturator nerve emerging from its lateral border

The obturator nerve and lumbosacral trunk emerge from the medial border.
Iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, lateral femoral cutaneous and femoral emerge laterally; genitofemoral anteriorly. (Last's)
Has the lumbar arteries passing beneath its fibrous arches

The four lumbar arteries and veins pass beneath the arches over the sides of the vertebral bodies.
They run laterally behind psoas with the sympathetic rami. (Last's)
Has quadratus lumborum in its posterior compartment

Quadratus lumborum is in the anterior compartment; erector spinae is in the posterior.
Three layers enclose the two compartments. (Last's)
Has three layers in the thoracic region

In the thoracic region there is only the posterior layer.
The anterior and middle layers exist only in the lumbar region. (Last's)
Has a middle layer attached to the bases of the lumbar transverse processes

The middle layer attaches to the tips of the transverse processes.
The anterior layer attaches to their bases, with the psoas fascia. (Last's)
Has its anterior and middle layers blending at the lateral border of quadratus lumborum

They blend there and give origin to transversus abdominis and internal oblique.
The posterior layer joins them at the lateral border of erector spinae. (Last's)
